title: What a Hard Breath Out Reveals
endLine: Each breath pays for recoil and airflow; disease changes either one.

scenes.tts: The first film showed a wet lining pulling each alveolus smaller, and surfactant easing that pull. Now breathe in fully and blow out hard. What does that blast reveal?
scenes.narration: The first film showed a wet lining pulling each alveolus smaller, and surfactant easing that pull. Now breathe in fully and blow out hard. What does that blast reveal?
scenes.caption: The first film showed a wet lining pulling each alveolus smaller, and surfactant easing that pull. Now breathe in fully and blow out hard. What does that blast reveal?
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's colour map: BLUE = air in the alveolus; YELLOW = the bare air-liquid surface; GREEN = surfactant lining; ORANGE = recoil pressure (the first film's pressure to hold an alveolus open); RED = the problem. New in this film: CYAN = pleural space and pleural pressure; WHITE = airflow arrows. ONE WORLD, kept all film. LEFT 60% of the frame, about 70% of its height, the 'lung panel': a thick GREY chest-wall arc around a thin CYAN pleural band; inside it one large BLUE alveolus with a GREEN rim on a single GREY airway tube that rises to a mouth opening at the top of the panel. Thin GREY spokes from the alveolar walls hold the airway tube round (tethers). ORANGE arrows on the alveolus rim point inward (recoil). At the far left, a vertical CYAN gauge labelled 'pleural pressure', scale -10 to +10 cmH2O, 0 marked 'atmospheric'; the part above 0 carries a small 'schematic' tag. RIGHT 40%, the 'spirogram panel': empty axes, x 'time (s)' 0 to 6, y 'volume out (L)' 0 to 3.5. Recap on the first sentence: a small ghost of the first film's two alveoli appears at top right of the lung panel with YELLOW inward tension arrows; on 'surfactant easing that pull' their rims turn GREEN and the arrows shrink; the ghost then dissolves into the large alveolus. Hook on 'blow out hard': the alveolus shrinks fast, big WHITE arrows burst out of the mouth, and a pen starts moving on the empty spirogram axes, then freezes. White text across the top: 'What does a hard blow reveal?'

Title 'What a Hard Breath Out Reveals' fades in above the lung panel for 2 s while the question text fades out. The alveolus breathes gently in and out; small WHITE arrows drift in and out of the mouth; the CYAN gauge needle sways between -5 and -8.

scenes.tts: Every breath has two pressure drops. Across the lung's wall, transpulmonary pressure matches the lung's recoil. Along the airways, a second drop moves the air. Pleural pressure pays for both.
scenes.narration: Every breath has two pressure drops. Across the lung's wall, transpulmonary pressure matches the lung's recoil. Along the airways, a second drop moves the air. Pleural pressure pays for both.
scenes.caption: Every breath has two pressure drops. Across the lung's wall, transpulmonary pressure matches the lung's recoil. Along the airways, a second drop moves the air. Pleural pressure pays for both.
scenes.visual: Quiet breathing continues, with the CYAN gauge needle swinging from -5 down to -8 cmH2O on each breath in and back (values from the lesson's quiet-breath table). On 'across the lung's wall', a short ORANGE double arrow spans the alveolar wall from inside to the CYAN pleural band, labelled 'transpulmonary = recoil'; it lengthens as the alveolus grows and shortens as it shrinks. On 'along the airways', a row of small WHITE arrows runs along the airway tube, labelled 'airway drop: moves air'. On 'pays for both', the CYAN gauge pulses and two thin CYAN lines run from it to the two labels, which glow together.

scenes.tts: Blow out hard, and the expiratory muscles push pleural pressure above atmospheric. Alveolar pressure is then recoil plus pleural pressure, and air rushes out.
scenes.narration: Blow out hard, and the expiratory muscles push pleural pressure above atmospheric. Alveolar pressure is then recoil plus pleural pressure, and air rushes out.
scenes.caption: Blow out hard, and the expiratory muscles push pleural pressure above atmospheric. Alveolar pressure is then recoil plus pleural pressure, and air rushes out.
scenes.visual: The quiet-breath labels fade. On 'blow out hard', the GREY chest-wall arc squeezes inward and the CYAN gauge needle climbs past 0 into the 'schematic' zone (no number). On 'recoil plus pleural pressure', a stacked bar grows beside the alveolus: an ORANGE block 'recoil' with a CYAN block 'pleural' on top, the whole bar labelled 'alveolar pressure' (heights schematic). On 'air rushes out', the alveolus shrinks steadily and thick WHITE arrows stream up the airway and out of the mouth.

scenes.tts: But the airways sit in the same pleural space. Friction uses up pressure along them, so toward the mouth the pressure inside keeps dropping. Where it drops to pleural pressure, the airway from there to the mouth is squeezed.
scenes.narration: But the airways sit in the same pleural space. Friction uses up pressure along them, so toward the mouth the pressure inside keeps dropping. Where it drops to pleural pressure, the airway from there to the mouth is squeezed.
scenes.caption: But the airways sit in the same pleural space. Friction uses up pressure along them, so toward the mouth the pressure inside keeps dropping. Where it drops to pleural pressure, the airway from there to the mouth is squeezed.
scenes.visual: Camera eases in so the airway tube and CYAN band fill most of the lung panel; the gauge stays in view. On 'same pleural space', the CYAN band around the airway brightens, with small inward CYAN arrows pressing on the tube. On 'friction uses up pressure', the inside of the tube fills with tiles shaded from bright (alveolus end) to dim (mouth end): pressure falling along the airway (schematic). On 'falls to pleural pressure', a white ring marks the tile whose shade matches the CYAN level, labelled 'inside = pleural'. On 'squeezed', the tube beyond the ring, toward the mouth, pinches narrow and turns RED, labelled 'squeezed'. WHITE arrows keep flowing through the pinch. On 'keeps dropping', a small WHITE arrow runs along the tiles toward the mouth, labelled 'pressure inside falls'. The cue 'falls to pleural pressure' is now 'drops to pleural pressure'.

scenes.tts: This is dynamic compression. Maximal flow is the fastest flow a hard blow out reaches. A weak recoil, or narrowed airways between the alveolus and the squeeze point, lowers it.
scenes.narration: This is dynamic compression. Maximal flow is the fastest flow a hard blow out reaches. A weak recoil, or narrowed airways between the alveolus and the squeeze point, lowers it.
scenes.caption: This is dynamic compression. Maximal flow is the fastest flow a hard blow out reaches. A weak recoil, or narrowed airways between the alveolus and the squeeze point, lowers it.
scenes.visual: Label 'dynamic compression' above the RED pinch. On 'a weak recoil', the ORANGE recoil arrows on the alveolus shrink and the WHITE flow arrows thin. They restore. On 'narrowed airways upstream', a stretch of the tube between the alveolus and the ring narrows (RED outline) and the WHITE arrows thin again. Label 'low maximal flow' appears beside the thin arrows. Both changes then reverse; camera eases back out to the full lung panel and spirogram panel. Direction only, no numbers. On 'maximal flow is the fastest flow', a small WHITE label 'maximal flow = fastest flow out' appears beside the WHITE arrows. The cue 'narrowed airways upstream' is now 'narrowed airways between'.

scenes.tts: A spirometer records the blast. F E V one is the volume out in the first second. F V C is the whole. In a made-up volunteer they are one point five and three litres. The ratio, zero point five, is below a made-up limit. Too small a share comes out in the first second: an obstructive pattern.
scenes.narration: A spirometer records the blast. FEV1 is the volume out in the first second. FVC is the whole. In a made-up volunteer they are 1.5 and 3.0 litres. The ratio, 0.50, is below a made-up limit. Too small a share comes out in the first second: an obstructive pattern.
scenes.caption: A spirometer records the blast. FEV1 is the volume out in the first second. FVC is the whole. In a made-up volunteer they are 1.5 and 3.0 litres. The ratio, 0.50, is below a made-up limit. Too small a share comes out in the first second: an obstructive pattern.
scenes.visual: The lung panel repeats a hard blow in sync with the pen. On the spirogram panel, a WHITE pen traces volume out against time, computed from the lesson's numbers: V(t) = 3.0 x (1 - 0.5^t) L, from t = 0 to 6 s (1.5 L at 1 s; 2.95 L at 6 s, flattening toward 3.0). On 'first second', a dashed vertical line at 1 s with a dot at 1.5 L, labelled 'FEV1 1.5 L'. On 'the whole', a dashed horizontal line at 3.0 L labelled 'FVC 3.0 L'. Tag at top of panel: 'volunteer 1 (made-up)'. On 'the ratio', a horizontal bar labelled 'FEV1/FVC = 0.50' grows from 0 to 0.50 on a 0 to 1 scale; a tick at 0.68 is labelled 'limit (made-up)'; the bar stops short of the tick and turns RED. On 'Obstructive', the word 'obstructive' stamps beside the bar. The stamped word reads 'obstructive: too little out in 1 s'.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. Pleural pressure pays for the lung's recoil and for moving air through the airways. Disease changes the recoil, or the resistance.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. Pleural pressure pays for the lung's recoil and for moving air through the airways. Disease changes the recoil, or the resistance.
scenes.caption: Here is the one idea. Pleural pressure pays for the lung's recoil and for moving air through the airways. Disease changes the recoil, or the resistance.
scenes.visual: The spirogram dims to 30% but stays. The lung panel returns to quiet breathing, CYAN needle swinging -5 to -8. On 'pays for', the CYAN gauge pulses; two CYAN lines run from it, one to the ORANGE recoil arrows on the alveolus (label 'recoil') and one along the airway's WHITE arrows (label 'resistance'). On 'Disease changes', each branch flickers in turn: the ORANGE arrows grow and shrink once; the airway narrows and widens once. Label under the lung panel: 'disease: recoil or resistance'.

scenes.tts: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, so recoil is too little, and maximal flow is low. Without walls tugging them open, small airways compress earlier. F E V one falls more than F V C, and the ratio falls.
scenes.narration: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, so recoil is too little, and maximal flow is low. Without walls tugging them open, small airways compress earlier. FEV1 falls more than FVC, and the ratio falls.
scenes.caption: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, so recoil is too little, and maximal flow is low. Without walls tugging them open, small airways compress earlier. FEV1 falls more than FVC, and the ratio falls.
scenes.visual: Label at top of the lung panel: 'emphysema: too little recoil'. On 'destroys alveolar walls', gaps open in the alveolus outline and the ORANGE recoil arrows shrink to stubs; the WHITE flow arrows thin. On 'without walls tugging them open', the GREY tether spokes around the airway fade one by one. On 'compress earlier', a hard blow runs: the RED pinch appears closer to the alveolus than before. On the spirogram, the volunteer-1 trace brightens again with its RED ratio bar, the tag changed to 'obstructive pattern' (no claim that volunteer 1 has emphysema). On 'the ratio falls', the RED bar pulses.

scenes.tts: Now fibrosis. Scarred tissue gives the lung too much recoil, and total lung capacity falls. Does its ratio of F E V one to F V C fall too?
scenes.narration: Now fibrosis. Scarred tissue gives the lung too much recoil, and total lung capacity falls. Does its ratio of FEV1 to FVC fall too?
scenes.caption: Now fibrosis. Scarred tissue gives the lung too much recoil, and total lung capacity falls. Does its ratio of FEV1 to FVC fall too?
scenes.visual: The emphysema changes reverse: walls close, tethers return. Label changes to 'fibrosis: too much recoil'. On 'scarred tissue', the alveolar wall and the spokes thicken into dense GREY, and the ORANGE recoil arrows grow large. On 'total lung capacity falls', the alveolus inflates to its largest size, which is visibly smaller than the adult's largest (a faint dashed outline shows the old size), labelled 'TLC falls'. The spirogram clears to empty axes. Question card at top in white: 'Does FEV1/FVC fall?'
Predict pause. The question card stays. The stiff alveolus breathes in small quick movements; the CYAN needle sways; the spirogram axes stay empty with a white '?' in the middle. No other change.

scenes.tts: No. High recoil drives high flow for the volume, and stiff tissue holds the airways open. F E V one and F V C fall together. The ratio is normal or high.
scenes.narration: No. High recoil drives high flow for the volume, and stiff tissue holds the airways open. FEV1 and FVC fall together. The ratio is normal or high.
scenes.caption: No. High recoil drives high flow for the volume, and stiff tissue holds the airways open. FEV1 and FVC fall together. The ratio is normal or high.
scenes.visual: The question card becomes 'No'. A hard blow runs on the stiff lung: large ORANGE arrows drive thick WHITE arrows out of the mouth; the thick GREY spokes hold the small airway round, and the RED pinch still forms but sits closer to the mouth than before. On the spirogram panel, two vertical bars labelled 'FEV1' and 'FVC' stand side by side, then shrink together by the same proportion (schematic, no numbers); the ratio bar beside them stays long, labelled 'normal or high'.

scenes.tts: That is the restrictive pattern: a low total lung capacity. A spirometer cannot see gas that never leaves the lung. One made-up volunteer had a normal ratio. A body box, a sealed booth that measures all the gas in the lung, found the low capacity.
scenes.narration: That is the restrictive pattern: a low total lung capacity. A spirometer cannot see gas that never leaves the lung. One made-up volunteer had a normal ratio. A body box, a sealed booth that measures all the gas in the lung, found the low capacity.
scenes.caption: That is the restrictive pattern: a low total lung capacity. A spirometer cannot see gas that never leaves the lung. One made-up volunteer had a normal ratio. A body box, a sealed booth that measures all the gas in the lung, found the low capacity.
scenes.visual: Label 'restrictive' stamps beside the fibrotic lung. On 'gas that never leaves', the alveolus deflates as far as it can, and a small BLUE core stays inside it, labelled 'never leaves'. On 'one made-up volunteer', the spirogram panel clears and the pen traces V(t) = 2.6 x (1 - 0.154^t) L (2.2 L at 1 s, flattening toward 2.6), tag 'volunteer 2 (made-up)', with 'FEV1 2.2 L', 'FVC 2.6 L' and a ratio bar 'FEV1/FVC = 0.85' labelled 'within limits'. On 'a body box', a GREY sealed box outline closes around the lung panel, labelled 'body box'; a bar 'TLC 3.9 L' appears on the spirogram panel beside a tick 'limit 4.6 L (made-up)', the bar short of the tick and RED. The body-box label reads 'body box: measures all the gas'.

scenes.tts: A newborn without enough surfactant has respiratory distress syndrome: too much surface recoil. Each breath needs a large negative swing in pleural pressure. That pulls the soft chest wall inward, and at low volume the alveoli close.
scenes.narration: A newborn without enough surfactant has respiratory distress syndrome: too much surface recoil. Each breath needs a large negative swing in pleural pressure. That pulls the soft chest wall inward, and at low volume the alveoli close.
scenes.caption: A newborn without enough surfactant has respiratory distress syndrome: too much surface recoil. Each breath needs a large negative swing in pleural pressure. That pulls the soft chest wall inward, and at low volume the alveoli close.
scenes.visual: The body box and spirogram fade; the lung panel resets to normal tissue and then scales down to a newborn's chest. Label 'RDS: too much surface recoil'. On 'enough surfactant', most of the GREEN rim turns bare YELLOW, and the ORANGE recoil arrows grow large. On 'large negative swing', the CYAN needle swings far below 0 on each breath in (no number, 'schematic'). On 'soft chest wall inward', the GREY chest-wall arc dents inward with each breath in, labelled 'retractions'. On 'alveoli close', at the end of a breath out the alveolus collapses flat, labelled 'alveoli close', then opens again with effort on the next breath.

scenes.tts: So read a sick lung by what each breath pays for. Emphysema, fibrosis and a surfactant-poor lung change the recoil. Asthma and chronic bronchitis narrow the airways.
scenes.narration: So read a sick lung by what each breath pays for. Emphysema, fibrosis and a surfactant-poor lung change the recoil. Asthma and chronic bronchitis narrow the airways.
scenes.caption: So read a sick lung by what each breath pays for. Emphysema, fibrosis and a surfactant-poor lung change the recoil. Asthma and chronic bronchitis narrow the airways.
scenes.visual: The lung panel returns to the adult lung with a GREEN rim, breathing quietly; the spirogram panel shows its empty axes. On 'what each breath pays for', the CYAN gauge pulses and its two branches light, 'recoil' and 'resistance'. On 'change the recoil', three tags slide in along the ORANGE recoil branch: 'emphysema', 'fibrosis', 'RDS'. On 'narrow the airways', a stretch of the airway upstream of the pinch site narrows in RED and two tags slide in along the resistance branch: 'asthma', 'chronic bronchitis'. The narrowing then relaxes.

End card over the dimmed but still moving world (the adult alveolus breathing quietly, the CYAN needle swaying between -5 and -8, small WHITE arrows in and out of the mouth). Large white text, centred: 'Each breath pays for recoil and airflow; disease changes either one.'
